reference.source: ICHD-3 / Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Caused by a non-iatrogenic spinal cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak leading to low CSF volume, and an important, treatable secondary cause of headache
The hallmark is an orthostatic headache that develops or worsens within minutes of standing or sitting and is relieved by lying flat, although the postural pattern can become less obvious over time
Associated symptoms include neck stiffness and pain, nausea, tinnitus, muffled hearing or aural fullness, photophobia, dizziness and interscapular pain

Underlying causes include a dural tear (often from a calcified disc or osteophyte), a meningeal diverticulum, or a CSF-venous fistula, and connective tissue disorders such as Marfan and Ehlers-Danlos syndromes predispose

Contrast-enhanced brain MRI classically shows diffuse smooth pachymeningeal enhancement, brain sagging, venous distension, subdural fluid collections and pituitary engorgement, summarised by the SEEPS mnemonic
Lumbar puncture opening pressure is often low but may be normal, so diagnosis rests on the clinical picture together with imaging rather than pressure measurement alone
Spinal imaging with CT or MR myelography, and dynamic or digital subtraction myelography, is used to localise the leak and in particular to detect a CSF-venous fistula

First-line treatment is conservative with bed rest, hydration and caffeine, followed by epidural blood patch, with targeted patching, fibrin glue or surgical or endovascular repair for refractory or localised leaks
reference.pathophysiology: A breach in the spinal dura allows CSF to escape into the epidural space or to drain into a vein as a CSF-venous fistula, reducing CSF volume. Because the cranium is a closed space, loss of CSF buoyancy allows the brain to descend, placing traction on pain-sensitive dura, bridging veins and cranial nerves and generating the headache and associated symptoms. In accordance with the Monro-Kellie doctrine, which holds that total intracranial volume is fixed, compensatory venous and dural engorgement produces the pachymeningeal enhancement, venous distension and pituitary enlargement seen on imaging. Low CSF volume, rather than pressure alone, is the key abnormality.
additionalDifferentials: Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and other orthostatic intolerance
Meningitis or meningeal carcinomatosis as other causes of dural enhancement
Subdural haematoma, which may itself be a complication
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis or raised intracranial pressure, which produce the opposite postural pattern
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced brain MRI for pachymeningeal enhancement, brain sagging, subdural collections and pituitary engorgement
Spinal MRI for extradural CSF collections and dilated nerve root sleeves
CT myelography or dynamic or digital subtraction myelography to localise the leak or a CSF-venous fistula
Lumbar puncture with opening pressure, which may be low or normal, and CSF analysis if infection or inflammation is considered
Heavily T2-weighted spinal imaging to help detect a CSF leak
Assessment for an underlying connective tissue disorder
redFlags: Deteriorating consciousness, a new focal deficit or seizures, which may indicate subdural haematoma or severe brain sagging
Features suggesting infection such as fever and meningism with systemic upset
Rapidly evolving brainstem signs from marked brain descent, which is a neurosurgical emergency
Development of a large or bilateral subdural haematoma
Thunderclap onset requiring exclusion of subarachnoid haemorrhage and other causes
reference.prognosis: Many patients improve with conservative measures or one or more epidural blood patches, and outcomes are generally good once the leak is treated. A subset have refractory leaks, particularly CSF-venous fistulas, requiring targeted or surgical intervention, and untreated severe cases can rarely progress to brain sagging with serious neurological deterioration.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because the lumbar puncture opening pressure is normal, which it often is
Misinterpreting diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement as meningitis or carcinomatosis
Not recognising that a longstanding leak may lose its clear postural character
Overlooking a CSF-venous fistula, which is missed by conventional myelography and needs a dynamic or lateral decubitus technique
Attributing an associated subdural haematoma to trauma and draining it without treating the underlying CSF leak
references: International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD-3)
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
